paragraphs.heading: Looking inside plants
paragraphs.text: Plant anatomy, also called phytotomy, is the study of the inside of plants. It once also covered plant morphology, the description of a plant's outward form, but since the mid-20th century it has been its own field dealing only with internal structure. Today it is often studied at the level of cells. The work often involves cutting tissues into sections and looking at them under a microscope.

paragraphs.heading: Early ideas
paragraphs.text: Around 300 BC, Theophrastus wrote several works on plants, of which only two survive. His ideas about plant form and classification did not hold up once Renaissance scientists examined them. In 1596 the Swiss physician and botanist Gaspard Bauhin published Pinax theatri botanici, the first work to name species with two-part names. He grouped plants by natural affinities, which were often a matter of structure.

paragraphs.heading: Two founders
paragraphs.text: Plant anatomy became a modern science in the late 1600s. The Italian doctor and microscopist Marcello Malpighi was one of its two founders, and he published Anatomia Plantarum in 1671. The other was the British doctor Nehemiah Grew, whose An Idea of a Philosophical History of Plants appeared in 1672. Grew is credited with recognizing plant cells, though he called them vesicles and bladders.

paragraphs.heading: Structure as a basis for order
paragraphs.text: In the 1700s Carl Linnaeus based his system of classification on structure, and his early work was in plant anatomy. He laid down its basic principles, even though views on which structures are worth comparing have shifted as knowledge grew. His major work, Species Plantarum, came out in 1753. In 1813 Augustin Pyrame de Candolle argued that anatomy, not physiology, should be the sole basis for classifying plants, and he set structural rules for telling genera apart.

paragraphs.heading: The cell comes into view
paragraphs.text: In 1802 Charles-François Brisseau de Mirbel published a treatise that marked the beginnings of plant cytology. Franz Meyen's Phytotomie, from 1830, was the first full review of plant anatomy. In 1838 Matthias Jakob Schleiden wrote that lower plants are single cells while higher plants are built from many cells. Eduard Strasburger described how plant cells divide by mitosis and showed that a new nucleus can only come from the division of an existing one.

paragraphs.heading: Tissues, fossils and evolution
paragraphs.text: Gottlieb Haberlandt sorted plant tissues by what they do. In his 1884 book Physiologische Pflanzenanatomie he described twelve types of tissue system, such as absorptive, mechanical and photosynthetic. At the end of the 19th century, two British paleobotanists, Dunkinfield Henry Scott and William Crawford Williamson, worked out how fossil plants were built. After Darwin's Origin of Species, Edward Charles Jeffrey used plant form and structure to trace evolutionary lines, and he published The Anatomy of Woody Plants in 1917.

paragraphs.heading: The modern textbooks
paragraphs.text: Agnes Arber led the growth of comparative plant anatomy, with books on water plants, monocotyledons and grasses published between 1920 and 1934. After World War II, Katherine Esau wrote Plant Anatomy, published in 1953. It became the definitive textbook on how plants are built, used in North American universities and elsewhere, and it was still in print in 2006. She followed it with Anatomy of Seed Plants in 1960.
